issues.legal_issue: A court considering whether to quash a criminal complaint cannot resolve disputed factual matters or assess disputed documents as though conducting a trial.
material_facts: The complaints alleged that land included in the agreements had already been sold before the agreements were made and that security cheques came from an account already closed.
The High Court disbelieved a schedule to an agreement because its pages were not paginated and decided the effect of a later agreement while considering petitions to quash the complaints.
The allegations and documents raised factual disputes requiring evidence at trial.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by resolving disputed facts at the quashing stage; the criminal proceedings should not have been quashed on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: The inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is to be exercised sparingly, including where the complaint itself does not disclose the alleged offences or where it is an abuse of process. A court considering quashing cannot record findings on disputed facts that require a full trial. The Court also considered the scope of that power as discussed in Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal (2007 (12) Scale 15).

predicates.appeal_from_criminal_complaint_quashing: The proceeding is an appeal from an order quashing a criminal complaint.
predicates.complaint_alleges_facts_constituting_off: The complaint alleges facts said to constitute criminal offences.
predicates.material_factual_disputes_require_eviden: The parties dispute material facts or documents that require evidence to resolve.
predicates.high_court_resolved_disputes_at_quashing: The High Court determined disputed facts or assessed disputed documents while considering whether to quash the complaint.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns quashing a complaint that alleges offences and material disputes require evidence, a High Court's resolution of those disputes at the quashing stage means quashing is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: The civil character of a contractual transaction and the existence of parallel civil or negotiable-instrument proceedings do not by themselves prevent criminal proceedings where fraud or cheating is alleged.
material_facts: The dispute arose from agreements to procure and transfer land in return for a substantial advance.
The complainant also pursued a civil recovery suit and a complaint concerning the security cheques.
The criminal complaints alleged cheating, fraud and conspiracy in connection with the agreements and payment.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit, the negotiable-instrument complaint, and the civil nature of the contract were not by themselves grounds to quash the criminal complaints.
issues.legal_principle: A contractual breach does not automatically amount to a criminal offence, but a contractual transaction may also involve criminal conduct if the required element of cheating or fraud is alleged. The existence of civil remedies or proceedings, including a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is by itself no ground to quash criminal proceedings. The Court considered S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar (2002) 1 SCC 241 and Anil Mahajan v. Bhor Industries Ltd. (2005) 10 SCC 228.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a later agreement novates an earlier contract, and the effect of any such novation, are matters for trial when they depend on disputed facts.
material_facts: The parties entered into an initial agreement and later entered into another agreement concerning the land transaction.
The High Court treated the later agreement as a novation when considering whether to quash the criminal complaints.
Whether the later agreement replaced the earlier agreement and what effect it had depended on disputed matters.
issues.conclusion: The existence and effect of any novation were to be considered after trial, not decided at the stage of an application to quash the complaints.
issues.legal_principle: Where the existence or effect of a later agreement depends on disputed facts, that issue is for determination after trial and cannot be conclusively resolved while exercising the power to quash a criminal complaint under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

issues.legal_issue: Allegations of dishonest intent at the time of a contractual transaction may support criminal prosecution even though the transaction also involves a breach of contract.
material_facts: The complaints alleged that some land promised under the agreements had already been sold before the agreements were entered into.
The complaints also alleged that security cheques were issued from an account that had been closed before the agreements.
The complainant alleged that the accused obtained an advance through fraudulent representations and failed to perform the agreements.
issues.conclusion: The allegations of prior sale and issuance of cheques from a previously closed account raised matters of dishonest intent that should be tried; the complaints could not be quashed merely because the dispute arose from a contract.
issues.legal_principle: Not every breach of contract is a criminal offence. However, breach of trust with mens rea, or fraudulent and dishonest intention at the time of the alleged offence, may give rise to criminal prosecution. Whether mens rea existed depends on the facts and complaint and is a matter for trial where disputed. The Court relied on S.W. Palanitkar v. State of Bihar (2002) 1 SCC 241 and Anil Mahajan v. Bhor Industries Ltd. (2005) 10 SCC 228.

issues.definition: When a complaint in a quashing appeal alleges dishonest intent at the time of a transaction and pre-existing facts inconsistent with the promise, the criminal allegations require trial.
